newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, China, Central Asia to cut border forces.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China, Central Asia to cut border forces.

text.p: The presidents of Russia, China, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan signed a pact on Thursday on troop reductions along the former Sino-Soviet border which they hope will prove a lasting model of regional security.

"This day will go down in history," Russia's Boris Yeltsin told China's Jiang Zemin, Kyrgyzstan's Askar Akayev, Kazakhstan's Nursultan Nazarbayev and Imomali Rakhmonov of Tajikistan before the signing ceremony.
"It took us seven years of tense talks to reach this result, which is unprecedented for Asia and the Pacific region," he said.

The treaty followed talks between Yeltsin and Jiang on Wednesday crowned by a declaration in which the two states outlined their vision of the post-Cold War world and voiced opposition to claims by any country for world leadership.

"No country should seek hegemony, practise power politics or monopolise international affairs," said the declaration. It did not mentioning any specific country but clearly had the United States in mind.

Moscow and Beijing see both the treaty and the declaration as part of their new relationship of "partnership aimed at strategic cooperation in the 21st century," but both sides ruled out any closer union.

"We have tried alliance and we have tried confrontation," said Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, referring to the Soviet-Chinese alliance of 1950s which collapsed into more than two decades of hostility.
"Both did not work and now we must find something else. "Our relations are not confrontational but they are not an alliance as well."

Soviet and Chinese forces clashed on the order in 1969, but relations between Beijing and Moscow have gradually improved since 1989 and the independent states left by the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 have established friendly relations with China.

No details of the treaty were officially disclosed. But Interfax news agency quoted Russian government experts as saying it would set limits to land forces, short-range aviation and anti-aircraft defences in a 100-km (63-mile) wide strip along the 7,500-km (4,700-mile) border.

The experts said the treaty would not affect strategic missile forces, long-range aviation units and or navy units in the area. They said Russia would cut its forces in the zone by 15 percent but gave no concrete figures.
The pact, which also includes a system of mutual inspections, is to be ratified by the parliaments of the five signatories.
"This is a good example of how to solve tricky and delicate national security issues through building up mutual confidence rather than by building up troops and expanding military blocs," Yeltsin.

Russia turned to China after its honeymoon with the West ended over NATO's decision to expand into eastern Europe, which Moscow sees as a security threat. But some Russian newspapers expressed doubts about the reproachement.

"So far it is difficult to say whether we need to plunge recklessly into a new alliance with the East just because we are not getting a proper hearing in the West," the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily said.

Jiang, who knows Russia's language and literature, will visit Yasnaya Polyana, the estate of 19th-century writer and philosopher Leo Tolstoy about 200 km (130 miles) south of Moscow, on Friday before leaving on Saturday.
